name: Xylitol mints

card.summary: Sugar-free mints sweetened with xylitol; only lab-model evidence so far.
card.note: Toxic to dogs; high intake can be laxative.

lead: Xylitol mints are breath mints sweetened with xylitol rather than sugar. People use them for fresher breath, to stimulate saliva and to cut sugar exposure on the teeth, which supports a cleaner mouth and a more confident close-up appearance. [1][2]

Xylitol is a sugar alcohol (E967) about as sweet as sucrose with roughly 40 percent fewer calories, and it has a very low glycemic index. [2] Wikipedia reports that a 2015 Cochrane review of ten studies found xylitol-containing fluoride toothpaste outperformed fluoride-only toothpaste, and that later reviews suggest xylitol suppresses pathogenic Streptococcus in the mouth. [2]

Direct evidence for mints is limited. A 2017 laboratory study in Current Microbiology used a dental simulator model to compare xylitol and sucrose mint products on Streptococcus mutans adherence and growth. [1] Wikipedia notes that a 2022 review found xylitol chewing gum reduces plaque but xylitol candy does not. [2]

chain: Mint stimulates saliva and gives fresh flavor
Xylitol is not fermented by oral bacteria as sucrose is
Fresher breath without feeding cavity-causing bacteria
angle.text: Mints give a quick flavor-based breath freshening, and using a xylitol-sweetened one avoids adding sugar for oral bacteria. Users reach for them after meals or before social situations.

infobox: Breath freshening, saliva stimulation, less sugar [2]
Xylitol (E967), about 2.4 kcal/g versus 4.0 for sugar [2]
One dental-simulator laboratory study of mint products [1]

paras: Emil Fischer and Rudolf Stahel isolated xylitol from beech wood in 1890, and sugar rationing in World War II renewed interest in sugar substitutes. [2] It has a glycemic index of about 7 percent that of glucose. [2]

For teeth, Wikipedia cites the 2015 Cochrane finding on xylitol toothpaste, reviews on suppression of pathogenic Streptococcus in the mouth, and a 2022 review in which xylitol gum reduced plaque and xylitol candy did not. [2]

High xylitol intake can cause gas, diarrhea and IBS-like symptoms, and the EU requires a laxative warning on products. [2] Xylitol is toxic to dogs, causing insulin release and potentially life-threatening hypoglycemia, with liver failure reported at doses above 500 mg/kg. [2] Higher intake increases urinary oxalate, calcium and phosphate, though a human kidney disease link has not been established. [2]

No studies found of xylitol mints in people. Related laboratory work: the 2017 dental-simulator study tested 3 percent solutions of sucrose, xylitol, sucrose mints, xylitol mints and peppermint oil on planktonic and adhered S. mutans. [1] Studies of xylitol chewing gum and toothpaste are described in the broader xylitol literature. [2]

quick.overview:
Xylitol mints are breath mints made with xylitol rather than sugar. Users choose them for fresh breath and saliva stimulation without sugar.

The only direct study is a 2017 laboratory simulator, and a 2022 review cited by Wikipedia found xylitol candy did not reduce plaque the way gum did.
quick.mechanism: Xylitol is thought to suppress oral streptococci, and sucking a mint stimulates saliva.
quick.risks: High intake can cause gas and diarrhea. Xylitol is toxic to dogs.
